https://www.euronews.com/2026/10/06/turk.text: Turkey and Pakistan will undertake a "rapid deployment" of troops to Saudi Arabia as part of a new mutual defence alliance, the three countries said Monday, as the Gulf kingdom faces escalating attacks from Yemen's Houthis.In August, the three countries signed the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement, committing to come to each other's aid if one were attacked.The pact unites NATO's second-largest army, that of Turkey, with the Islamic world's only nuclear-armed state, Pakistan, and the largest Gulf power, Saudi Arabia.Their representatives held an emergency meeting in Riyadh on Monday, where they noted recent attacks on Saudi Arabia, in particular those targeting the holy cities of Mecca and Medina, without mentioning the Tehran-backed Houthis by name.The trio "reaffirmed their unequivocal rejection of any attack or threat against the kingdom's security and territorial integrity", they said in a joint statement.They also agreed "to move immediately to the practical implementation of the collective defence commitments and to take the necessary measures to provide the agreed military forces and capabilities and ensure their rapid deployment in the kingdom".The statement did not specify what sort of role the troops would fill once in Saudi Arabia.Saudi Arabia has faced repeated Houthi attacks targeting its cities, oil infrastructure and ships ever since Yemen's civil war flared back to life in July.In September, the group launched a new offensive that seized swathes of territory from Yemen's internationally recognised government, which on Monday launched a counteroffensive with Riyadh's support, seeking to retake all Houthi territory, some of it held for more than a decade.

Photograph: Yoruk Isik/Reuters View image in fullscreen The Agioi Fanendes, a Malta-flagged medium-sized tanker, seen here in Turkey in 2024, is reportedly one of three diesel tankers headed from Russia to the US. Photograph: Yoruk Isik/Reuters Russia-Ukraine war at a glance Russia Explainer Ukraine war briefing: Russian diesel tankers headed for North America, says Moscow, as US tries to revive peace talks Tankers part of US-Russia deal that could see 500,000 metric tonnes of fuel supplied to world market this month. What we know on day 1,704 Guardian staff and agencies Fri 23 Oct 2026 21.20 EDT Last modified on Fri 23 Oct 2026 21.21 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Three tankers carrying Russian diesel are on their ⁠way to North America, Russian deputy prime minister Alexander Novak said ⁠on Friday . In ​a statement quoted by Russian news agencies, Novak said the cargoes were ⁠part of a deal that could see Russian companies supply 500,000 metric tonnes to US and world markets in October. “The first ⁠three fuel tankers are already on their ​way to the eastern ‌coast of ‌the Atlantic Ocean, with significant support from the ‌RDIF (Russian Direct Investment Fund),” Novak said. Under a deal announced this month by US president Donald Trump, Russia agreed ‌to supply diesel to global markets in an effort to lower fuel ​prices in return for Trump temporarily lifting US sanctions on Russian fuel. Reuters reported that the Malta-flagged ⁠medium-sized tanker Agioi Fanendes, loaded with ultra-low sulphur diesel, is expected to arrive in ‌the US on 7 November. The White House has said that Russia and Ukraine have agreed to a ceasefire in the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky , where a deepening humanitarian crisis has left thousands of civilians struggling to survive. In a statement on Friday, the White House said both sides had agreed to halt all military operations in the city from 27 October to allow humanitarian aid deliveries and preparations for the evacuation of civilians. Residents of the southern Ukrainian city, which has been under Russian occupation since February 2022, have described increasingly desperate conditions amid severe shortages of food, water and electricity. An estimated 2,000 people remain in the city, with some reportedly forced to survive on weeds, boiled grass, bread and meagre rations. Both Russian and Ukrainian officials said all sides were close to agreeing to a ceasefire. The Oleshky ceasefire comes as the US is trying to organise new talks aimed at ending the war . Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Friday negotiators from Ukraine, Russia and the US have agreed to technical-level meetings in the first half of November in Abu Dhabi. A US official later said the three ⁠countries may hold their next talks in a couple weeks in Abu Dhabi or Switzerland. Zelenskyy said he hoped a meeting of the countries’ leaders would follow. The peace efforts follow a rift between Washington and Kyiv in recent weeks and a series of moves by Trump seen as favouring Russia, including limitations being placed on the Starlink communication system that Ukraine uses to protect against incoming attacks. Trump said on Friday that if Ukraine still faced a problem accessing the system, he would straighten it out ​and, if necessary, speak about the matter to SpaceX CEO Elon Musk. As the UK government prepares next week for the first budget under Andy Burnham’s leadership, EU leaders have pressed the new prime minister at a summit in Brussels to contribute more to Ukraine’s defence effort . EU officials say Canada and Japan also should do more to support Ukraine . The UN nuclear watchdog IAEA said ⁠Fiday ​that repairs to key ⁠power infrastructure near Ukraine’s Zaporizhzhia ⁠nuclear power ​plant ‌had been completed ‌ under a ‌temporary ceasefire it brokered. The repairs strengthened the plant’s connection ‌to its sole remaining external power ​line, known as Ferosplavna-1, reducing the ⁠risk of another ​loss of ​off-site ​electricity at ​Europe’s largest ‌nuclear ​power ​station. https://www.politico.eu/article/frontex-.text: BRUSSELS — The European Commission will unveil a sweeping overhaul of EU border agency Frontex on Oct. 27, turning it into a fully-fledged “European return agency,” according to two EU officials familiar with the proposal. The legislative proposal, which will revamp the Warsaw-based agency’s mandate, will focus on three key areas: strengthening its role in deportations, improving its ability to anticipate and respond to border crises, and boosting its operational capacity without poaching border guards from countries. At the heart of the reform is an ambition to give Frontex a much more prominent role in returning people with no legal right to remain in the EU, including new powers to carry out return operations beyond the bloc’s territory, said the officials, who were granted anonymity to discuss information not yet in the public domain. Advertisement Advertisement The push comes just months after EU lawmakers approved a new “return regulation” aimed at accelerating deportations and allowing member countries to establish controversial deportation hubs outside the EU. With the legal framework largely agreed, Brussels is now turning its attention to enforcement — and to the agency expected to help make the new rules work in practice. Political pressure has also been mounting. In June, the leaders of 19 EU countries urged the Commission to support the establishment of return hubs outside the bloc, including through EU funding, as first reported by POLITICO . The proposed Frontex overhaul, which is on the College of Commissioners’ agenda and is expected to be approved by the EU executive on Oct. 27, would help put that broader shift into practice by giving the agency more resources, greater operational flexibility and an expanded role in carrying out returns beyond EU borders, including transfers between third countries. Emergency response But deportations are only part of the equation. The Commission also wants to transform Frontex into a force that can intervene in border emergencies within 24 hours, according to the two officials. Advertisement Advertisement The ambition stems partly from the lessons of the Ceuta migration crisis , which exposed gaps in Europe’s ability to anticipate and respond to sudden pressure at its external borders. Brussels wants to ensure that a similar crisis doesn’t catch the EU off guard again. Under the plans, Frontex would be given a stronger mandate to monitor potential flashpoints, particularly on social media, and improve early warning capabilities and identify emerging threats before they escalate. The agency would also be better equipped to respond swiftly once a crisis happens, with personnel and equipment available for deployment on short notice rather than relying exclusively on existing arrangements with national governments. Staffing questions Another central question is how big Frontex should become. The agency had around 7,800 personnel in its Standing Corps in early 2026 and is working towards a target of 10,000 by 2027. Commission President Ursula von der Leyen has previously called for tripling that figure to 30,000 European border and coast guards. The Commission’s proposal is expected to seek a compromise between the competing ambitions for expansion and the practical constraints facing national governments. Advertisement Advertisement Rather than relying entirely on a substantially larger permanent force, Brussels is considering a sizeable reserve that officials say could be mobilized when needed. That would help address countries’ concerns that an expanded EU-level force could pull their border guards away at a time when national authorities are already under pressure. The approach would allow Frontex to increase its deployable capacity while keeping more personnel available for national duties when they are not needed for European operations. Beyond staffing, the two people expect the Commission to put forward measures to give the agency better equipment and more agile operational procedures, particularly for deportations. The reform is also likely to reopen debates over the agency’s accountability and human rights of migrants and asylum-seekers, especially as the EU moves towards more deportations to third countries. Frontex did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
